citeAs: Welbl, J., Liu, N. F., & Gardner, M. (2017). Crowdsourcing Multiple Choice Science Questions. arXiv:1707.06209.
creator: Johannes Welbl (University College London), Nelson F. Liu (University of Washington), Matt Gardner (Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence)
description: SciQ is a dataset of 13,679 multiple choice science exam questions crowdsourced using a novel two-step method that leverages domain-specific textbooks and model-generated answer distractor suggestions. Each question includes a question, four answer options (one correct and three distractors), and an associated passage from a science textbook used to formulate the question. The dataset covers biology, chemistry, earth science, and physics topics spanning elementary to college introductory level.
name: SciQ
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each question was handled by at least two workers: one for question formulation and one for distractor selection/validation. The distractor selection worker also performed quality control validation.
rai:annotatorDemographics: A total of 175 workers participated in the crowdsourcing project. All workers were required to have Amazon Mechanical Turk Master's status. No further demographic information (age, gender, nationality, education) is provided.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: A qualitative evaluation was conducted: 100 original science exam questions and 100 SciQ crowdsourced questions were presented to human judges who were asked to identify which was the real exam question. Judges identified the real exam question in only 55% of cases, which falls below the significance level of p=0.05 under a null hypothesis of random guessing, indicating the crowdsourced questions are indistinguishable from real exam questions. Additionally, 92.8% of questions passed the quality control step in the distractor selection task.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Two-step crowdsourcing process: (1) Question Formulation Task — workers were shown three filtered textbook paragraphs, chose one (or rejected all), and wrote a science exam question with a correct answer. Instructions specified: no yes/no questions, questions must not require further context, should query general principles, question length 6-30 words, answer length up to 3 words, no ambiguous questions. Examples of desirable and undesirable questions were provided. Workers were paid $0.30 per HIT and required AMT Master's status. (2) Distractor Selection Task — a second worker validated the (question, answer) pair (marking it as ungrammatical, false answer, unrelated to science, or requiring very specific knowledge), then selected up to two of six model-suggested distractors and wrote at least one distractor themselves. Workers were paid $0.20 per HIT and required AMT Master's status. 92.8% of questions passed quality control.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset is intentionally domain-targeted toward science exam topics (biology, chemistry, earth science, physics) at elementary to college introductory level. The base corpus was deliberately chosen to avoid overly specific facts (e.g., Simple Wikipedia was rejected for being too specific) and commercial/irrelevant documents (web search results were rejected). The question distribution was designed to resemble real science exam questions rather than cloze-style or automatically generated questions.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected via a two-step crowdsourcing process on Amazon Mechanical Turk. In the first step, crowd workers were shown three filtered textbook paragraphs, chose one, and wrote a question answerable from that passage along with a correct answer. In the second step, a different worker validated the question and selected or wrote three answer distractors, aided by model-generated distractor suggestions. A total of 175 workers participated. The total budget was $10,415. The base corpus consisted of 28 science study textbooks from CK-12 and OpenStax covering biology, chemistry, earth science, and physics.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: 28 science study textbooks from CK-12 and OpenStax, covering biology, chemistry, earth science, and physics, spanning elementary level to college introductory material. CK-12 books were obtained under the Creative Commons Attribution-Non-Commercial 3.0 Unported (CC BY-NC 3.0) License. A set of 3,705 real science exam questions (4th and 8th grade) was used to train the distractor model.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, Document analysis
rai:dataLimitations: A small percentage of passages were obtained from unreleasable texts, so the direct-answer version of SciQ is slightly smaller (10,481 train, 887 dev, 884 test) than the multiple choice version. Neural models do not beat simple information retrieval baselines on the multiple choice version, suggesting limitations in the complexity of reasoning required. The distractor model quality is not high enough to use predictions directly without additional filtering by crowd workers.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset was randomly shuffled and split into training, validation, and test portions, with 1,000 questions in each of the validation and test sets and the remainder in the training set (totaling 13,679 questions). 36.1% of the distractors in the final dataset were generated by the distractor model (workers could select up to two of six predicted distractors and were required to write at least one themselves).
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A rule-based document filter was applied to textbook paragraphs to select suitable passages for question generation. The filter classified individual sentences and accepted a paragraph if a minimum number of sentences passed. Sentences were filtered out if they: (i) were a question or exclamation, (ii) had no verb phrase, (iii) contained modal verbs, (iv) contained imperative phrases, (v) contained demonstrative pronouns, (vi) contained personal pronouns other than third-person, (vii) began with a pronoun, (viii) contained first names, (ix) had fewer than 6 or more than 18 tokens or more than 2 commas, (x) contained special characters other than punctuation, (xi) had more than three tokens beginning uppercase, (xii) mentioned a graph, table or web link, (xiii) began with a discourse marker, (xiv) contained absolute wording (e.g., 'never', 'nothing', 'definitely'), or (xv) contained instructional vocabulary ('teacher', 'worksheet', etc.).
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset addresses the bottleneck of limited in-domain training data for science exam question answering, enabling progress on high-level NLP tasks requiring information extraction, reading comprehension, and common sense reasoning. It provides a resource for studying neural model performance in medium-data settings and for improving AI performance on science education tasks.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for: (1) training and evaluating models on multiple choice science exam question answering; (2) studying neural reading comprehension models in medium-sized data settings (tens of thousands of examples); (3) augmenting training data for answering real 4th and 8th grade science exam questions; (4) a direct-answer reading comprehension task where a model must predict the answer span from a given passage.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: A random forest classifier (trained using scikit-learn with 500 trees and at least 4 samples per tree leaf) was used to rank and suggest answer distractors for each question-answer pair. The model was trained on 3,705 real science exam questions (80% train, 20% validation split) and used features including GloVe embeddings, POS-tag consistency, WordNet hypernymy indicators, and OpenIE-based knowledge base links. The candidate distractor set contained 488,819 expressions including the 400K GloVe vocabulary items.
